fixes.explanation: Right, baker. Every flood line in this psalm is a "would have," like "…then the floods would have engulfed us… then the raging waters would have swept us away." (Psalm 124:4-5). David is telling what would have happened if the LORD had not been on their side (Psalm 124:1). Then he blesses the LORD, who "…has not given us as prey to their teeth." (Psalm 124:6).

Soldiers watching for a signal is a good picture, and I can see why you picked it. But the singer doesn't use it. He says, "As the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master…" (Psalm 123:2). These are servants, friend, not soldiers, and their eyes are on a master's hand.

Waiting for the morning is a real kind of waiting, and I see why you picked it. But this singer doesn't say that. He says their eyes are on the LORD "…until He shows us mercy." (Psalm 123:2). The wait ends with mercy, friend, not with the sunrise.

Contempt is right, baker. The singer says, "Have mercy on us, O LORD, have mercy, for we have endured much contempt." (Psalm 123:3). The next verse says it comes "…from the arrogant…" and "…from the proud." (Psalm 123:4). Being looked down on like that is heavy, and I think that's why the asking is so loud.

Right, baker. Psalm 123 closes with "We have endured much scorn from the arrogant, much contempt from the proud." (Psalm 123:4). These verses show no answer from the LORD, and they never say the scorn stopped. The song ends on the asking.
Egypt is a big name in the Bible, but it's not in this line. David says, "…let Israel now declare…" (Psalm 124:1). The ones called to declare are Israel, friend, not Egypt.

True! David says that without the LORD on their side, "…they would have swallowed us alive…" (Psalm 124:3). He says it right after "…when their anger flared against us…" (Psalm 124:3). Notice it's a what-if, baker. He's telling you what would have happened without the LORD on their side, and it's a scary picture.

Chaff in the wind is a vivid picture, but it's not this one. David says the LORD "…has not given us as prey to their teeth." (Psalm 124:6). So it's teeth, baker. Nobody's getting blown around in this verse.

A bird from the snare, that's right! David says, "We have escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowler…" (Psalm 124:7). A fowler is someone who traps birds. So the picture is a bird slipping out of the trapper's snare.

Strength in a king is a fair guess, friend. But David points somewhere else. He says, "Our help is in the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth." (Psalm 124:8). The help is in the LORD's name, baker, not in a king.
